⚠️ Read First: Which Exam This Prepares You For

The current, widely-accepted TOGAF fundamentals certification is TOGAF® Enterprise Architecture Foundation — exam code OGEA-101 — based on the TOGAF Standard, 10th Edition. The older "TOGAF 9 Foundation" exam still exists but is legacy; new candidates should register for OGEA-101.

Exam format (identical for both editions): 40 multiple-choice questions · 60 minutes · 60% pass mark (24/40 correct) · delivered via Pearson VUE.

About 85–90% of this study material applies directly to OGEA-101. The Architecture Development Method (ADM), ADM techniques, "Applying the ADM," architecture governance, architecture content (deliverables, artifacts, building blocks), and core concepts/definitions are essentially unchanged between TOGAF 9.2 and the 10th Edition — and that is where most exam marks are.

What is DIFFERENT in the 10th Edition (flagged throughout this guide with a 🔟 10th Edition note):

Topic TOGAF 9.2 (older framing used in this guide) TOGAF 10 / OGEA-101 (current exam)
Document structure "7 Parts" (Parts I–VII) TOGAF Fundamental Content (6 documents) + TOGAF Series Guides + TOGAF Library (see Day 2)
Reference Models (TRM, III-RM) In the core; ~5–8% of exam Moved to a Series Guide; NOT on the OGEA-101 Foundation syllabus — learn the concept lightly, don't over-invest
Enterprise Continuum / Views & Viewpoints Standalone exam topics Still valid concepts (under "Architecture Content" / "Concepts & Definitions") but less prominent as standalone topics
OGEA-101 syllabus areas — Intro to ADM · ADM Techniques · Applying the ADM · Architecture Governance · Architecture Content · TOGAF Certification Program · Concepts & Definitions

Wherever this guide says "Part II / Part IV / 7 Parts," mentally map it to the 10th-Edition equivalent (mapping table in Day 2). The underlying concepts are identical — only the packaging changed. Everything in this guide remains useful; the notes simply re-point the emphasis toward what OGEA-101 actually tests.

Day 1: TOGAF Definition, Purpose & History

What is TOGAF?

TOGAF stands for The Open Group Architecture Framework.

Definition (Official):

TOGAF is a framework and methodology for developing enterprise architectures. It enables organizations to design, evaluate, and build the right architecture for addressing business needs.

Purpose:
TOGAF solves a common enterprise problem: How do you design systems that align with business strategy, integrate across departments, are scalable, maintainable, and cost-effective?

Without TOGAF (or similar framework):

  • Architects design in silos
  • Systems don't communicate
  • Technical debt accumulates
  • Business strategy doesn't translate to IT
  • Change management is chaotic

With TOGAF:

  • Architects follow a structured method (ADM)
  • Systems are designed with integration in mind
  • Technical decisions trace back to business goals
  • Change is planned and managed
  • Reusable components reduce waste

TOGAF History & Context

  • Developed by: The Open Group — a vendor-neutral standards consortium (not a software company); members include IBM, Microsoft, Oracle, HP, and 800+ others. Its purpose is to create open, vendor-neutral standards.
  • First version: TOGAF 1.0 (1995), derived from the US Department of Defense TAFIM framework
  • Current version for this exam: TOGAF 9.2 (released April 2018) — the Level 1 exam is based on TOGAF 9.2
  • Latest version: TOGAF 10 (released April 2022) — a significant update; this guide covers 9.2 which is what the certification tests
  • Adoption: Used by 80%+ of Fortune 500 companies; the world's most widely adopted enterprise architecture framework
  • Standards alignment: Complements ITIL (service management), COBIT (IT governance), Six Sigma (process quality) — TOGAF does not replace these

Why Enterprises Use TOGAF

  1. Alignment — Business strategy → IT strategy → architecture
  2. Standardization — Consistent approach across all architecture efforts
  3. Communication — Common language for architects, executives, technical staff
  4. Governance — Decision frameworks, roles, approval processes
  5. Reusability — Building blocks, reference models, lessons learned
  6. Risk management — Structured evaluation of alternatives, impact analysis
  7. Cost reduction — Eliminates redundant systems, standardizes platforms

TOGAF in Your Context (Saudi Market)

In Saudi Arabia:

  • Vision 2030 digitalization initiatives require enterprise architecture
  • Government and large enterprises adopt TOGAF for major transformation programs
  • Enterprise architects with TOGAF are highly valued
  • Architecture boards use TOGAF as governance framework
  • Integration projects (ERP, cloud, consolidation) require TOGAF methodology

Your advantage: 20+ years designing large-scale systems + TOGAF certification = highly attractive in Saudi market.

Key Takeaway for Day 1

TOGAF is not a specific technology or tool. It's a methodology and framework for thinking about, designing, and governing enterprise architecture.

Day 2: TOGAF Structure — The "Parts" of TOGAF

TOGAF is divided into several logical parts. Understanding this structure helps you navigate the framework and the exam.

The TOGAF 9.2 Document Structure

TOGAF 9.2 is formally organized into 7 parts. For the Level 1 exam, you need to know 6 of them. They are often taught as 4 key areas — but know the full structure to avoid being caught out.

🔟 10th Edition note — the structure the OGEA-101 exam actually tests: TOGAF 10 replaced the "7 Parts" with three groupings:

  • TOGAF Fundamental Content — the examinable core, 6 documents: (1) Introduction & Core Concepts, (2) Architecture Development Method (ADM), (3) ADM Techniques, (4) Applying the ADM, (5) Architecture Content, (6) Enterprise Architecture Capability & Governance
  • TOGAF Series Guides — focused topic guides (Business Architecture, Information Architecture, Security Architecture, the Leader's Guide, and the Reference Models incl. TRM & III-RM, etc.)
  • TOGAF Library — a wider body of supporting reference material

Mapping from the 7 Parts to the 10th-Edition Fundamental Content:

9.2 Part 10th-Edition equivalent
Part I: Introduction Introduction & Core Concepts
Part II: ADM Architecture Development Method (ADM)
Part III: ADM Guidelines & Techniques ADM Techniques + Applying the ADM
Part IV: Architecture Content Framework Architecture Content
Part V: Enterprise Continuum & Tools folded into Architecture Content
Part VI: Reference Models (TRM, III-RM) moved to a Series Guide (not Foundation-examined)
Part VII: Architecture Capability Framework Enterprise Architecture Capability & Governance

The 7-Parts framing below is still an excellent way to learn the concepts — just memorise the 10th-Edition document names too, since OGEA-101's "Concepts & Definitions" and "TOGAF Certification Program" areas test the document classification.

Part I: Introduction

  • What: Defines key terms, concepts, and what TOGAF is
  • Exam focus: Terminology tested throughout the exam

Part II: Architecture Development Method (ADM) ← Most Important

  • What: The step-by-step process for developing enterprise architecture
  • Contains: 9 phases (Preliminary, A–H) + Requirements Management at the center
  • Purpose: Provides a repeatable, governance-controlled approach to architecture
  • Exam focus: ~60% of the exam tests ADM phases, inputs, outputs, activities

Part III: ADM Guidelines & Techniques

  • What: How to adapt/customize ADM for your organization
  • Contains: Customization options, how to add/skip phases, iteration guidance
  • Purpose: Allows tailoring of ADM to match organizational culture and maturity
  • Exam focus: ~5% of the exam

Part IV: Architecture Content Framework

  • What: The taxonomy and structure of architecture content
  • Contains: Metamodel, Building Blocks (ABB/SBB), artifact types, deliverables
  • Purpose: Defines what goes into architecture — what to produce and how to organize it
  • Exam focus: ~10% of the exam

Part V: Enterprise Continuum & Tools ← Don't Skip

  • What: A classification system for architectures from generic to organization-specific
  • Contains: Architecture Continuum, Solutions Continuum, Architecture Repository
  • Purpose: Explains how organizations reuse and leverage reference architectures
  • Key concept: Foundation → Common Systems → Industry → Organization-Specific
  • Exam focus: ~10% of the exam; Enterprise Continuum questions appear regularly

Part VI: TOGAF Reference Models

  • What: Pre-built example architectures as starting points
  • Contains: Foundation Architecture (FA / TRM), Integrated Information Infrastructure Reference Model (III-RM)
  • Purpose: Give you a head start; use as templates rather than building from scratch
  • Exam focus: ~5% on the legacy TOGAF 9 exam. 🔟 10th Edition note: the reference models were moved to a Series Guide and are not on the OGEA-101 Foundation syllabus — read this part for understanding, but don't spend heavy memorisation time on it if you're sitting OGEA-101.

Part VII: Architecture Capability Framework ← Don't Skip

  • What: How to establish and run an architecture practice
  • Contains: Architecture Board setup, Architecture Governance, Architecture Contracts, Architecture Maturity Models, Skills Framework
  • Purpose: Defines roles, responsibilities, governance mechanisms for enterprise architecture
  • Exam focus: ~10% of the exam; Architecture Board and governance questions appear regularly

What's Mandatory vs. Optional?

Element Status Notes
Using the ADM as your method Core The ADM is the heart of TOGAF; using it is the expected approach
Using all 9 phases in every cycle Adaptable You may combine, abbreviate, or focus phases to fit the specific initiative
Following the standard phase sequence Adaptable The default sequence is recommended; it can be tailored, with justification
Architecture Content Framework Recommended Helps organize artifacts; not strictly required
Enterprise Continuum Recommended Use to classify and reuse architectures
Reference Models (TRM, III-RM) Optional Use if applicable to your domain
Customizing/tailoring TOGAF Expected TOGAF explicitly expects you to tailor it to your context (done in the Preliminary Phase)

Key Point: TOGAF is prescriptive but flexible. The ADM itself is central — you are expected to use it — but how you apply it (which phases, what sequence, what depth) is tailored to your organization. You follow the spirit of the ADM, but customize the letter to match your context.

Key Takeaway for Day 2

TOGAF 9.2 has 7 parts. Part II (ADM) is ~60% of the exam. Parts V and VII (Enterprise Continuum and Architecture Capability Framework) are also tested — don't skip them.

Day 3: Architecture Development Method (ADM) — 9 Phases Overview

Today, we'll zoom out and see the 9-phase ADM cycle from 10,000 feet. Each phase has a purpose, inputs, and outputs.

The 9 ADM Phases (In Sequence)

Preliminary Phase: Framework & Governance

  • Goal: Set up the architecture practice; customize TOGAF for the organization; establish governance
  • When: Before any specific architecture project begins — done once, then periodically updated
  • Key Activity: Define the rules of the game before playing a single game

Formal Inputs:

  • TOGAF library (the framework itself)
  • Existing organizational model for enterprise architecture (if any)
  • Board strategies, business goals, business drivers
  • Existing governance and legal frameworks
  • Other architecture frameworks in use (Zachman, FEAF, etc.)

Formal Outputs:

  • Organizational Model for Enterprise Architecture — defines scope, roles, responsibilities, and budget for the EA function
  • Tailored Architecture Framework — TOGAF customized to fit the organization's methods, tools, and terminology
  • Architecture Principles — the fundamental governance rules that guide all architecture decisions throughout every ADM phase; have 4 components: Name, Statement, Rationale, Implications
  • Initial Architecture Repository — the storage system for all architecture artifacts, populated with initial content
  • Architecture Governance Framework — defines how architecture decisions are made, who approves, how compliance is enforced

Exam tip — Architecture Principles (4 components):

  • Name — short label representing the rule (e.g., "Data is an Asset")
  • Statement — unambiguous declaration of the fundamental rule
  • Rationale — why the principle matters; the business benefits of following it
  • Implications — what following this principle requires from business and IT

Example: Principle "Technology Independence"

  • Statement: "Applications shall not be dependent on specific technology platforms"
  • Rationale: Reduces vendor lock-in; enables technology evolution
  • Implications: Requires abstraction layers; increases initial development effort

Architecture Principles are established in the Preliminary Phase and applied in every subsequent phase. Phase A confirms they still apply to the current initiative.

Exam tip — What triggers Phase A? The Preliminary Phase may produce a "Request for Architecture Work" to kick off Phase A. Alternatively, a Request for Architecture Work can be issued directly by business/IT leadership. Either way, the Request for Architecture Work formally starts Phase A.

Phase A: Architecture Vision

  • Goal: Define the problem and desired state; get formal approval to proceed
  • Key Deliverables:
    • Architecture Vision — high-level description of target capabilities and business value (NOT a detailed design)
    • Statement of Architecture Work — the formal project charter; defines scope, schedule, resources; must be signed by the Architecture Sponsor before Phase B begins
  • Other Outputs: Business Case, Stakeholder Map & Concerns, Communications Plan, refined Architecture Principles
  • Key Activity: Identify stakeholders and concerns; define scope; develop Architecture Vision; secure formal approval via Statement of Architecture Work

Exam tip: Two documents often confused: "Architecture Vision" describes the target state. "Statement of Architecture Work" is the project charter. Both are Phase A outputs. Phase B cannot start without the Statement of Architecture Work being approved.

Phase B: Business Architecture

  • Goal: Design the Business Architecture — the first and most important domain; all other domains are driven by it
  • Key Deliverables:
    • Business Capability Map — hierarchical view of what the organization can do
    • Business Process Models (AS-IS and TO-BE) — how processes work today and how they should work
    • Gap Analysis Results — what needs to change; becomes candidate roadmap components
  • Other Outputs: Organizational Structure Diagrams, Business Interaction Matrix, Business Goals Catalogue, Business Architecture sections of the Architecture Definition Document (ADD)
  • Key Activity: Document AS-IS and design TO-BE business architecture; perform Gap Analysis; begin building the ADD

Phase C: Information Systems Architecture

  • Goal: Design the data and application landscape that supports the Business Architecture from Phase B

  • Key Deliverables: Logical data model, application portfolio map, application interface catalog

  • Outputs: Data architecture (logical — NOT physical; physical data models are project-level, not EA-level), application architecture, data flow diagrams, Information Systems Architecture sections of the ADD

  • Key Activity: Design data entities and flows (Data Architecture sub-phase); then design applications and interfaces (Application Architecture sub-phase); add to the ADD

  • Important: Phase C has two sub-phases, always in this order:

    1. Data Architecture first — design data entities, relationships, flows, and governance
    2. Application Architecture second — design applications that consume and produce the data

    This ordering matters: you must know what data exists before you can correctly design the applications that use it. Exam questions test this sequencing.

Exam tip: Phase C produces logical data models (technology-independent, conceptual). Physical data models (specific tables, columns, indexes for a particular database) are created at project level during implementation — NOT at enterprise architecture level.

Phase D: Technology Architecture

  • Goal: Design the infrastructure to run applications and data
  • Key Deliverables: Technology standards, platform stack, infrastructure diagrams
  • Outputs: Technology roadmap, standards, deployment architecture
  • Key Activity: Choose platforms, tools, infrastructure components

Phase E: Opportunities & Solutions

  • Goal: Consolidate all Gap Analysis results from Phases B, C, D; group into Work Packages; produce the first complete Architecture Roadmap
  • Key Deliverables:
    • Work Package List — bundles of related implementation activities, each with scope, dependencies, cost, and benefit
    • Transition Architecture(s) — stable intermediate states between AS-IS and TO-BE, enabling phased delivery without stranding the organization
    • Architecture Roadmap v0.1 — first integrated, complete roadmap across all 4 domains; consolidates candidate components from Phases B, C, D
    • Implementation and Migration Plan v0.1 — initial view of what will be built and when
  • Key Activity: Integrate three domain gap analyses into coherent work packages; define transition states; produce the first complete roadmap

Exam tip: Transition Architectures are first defined in Phase E, not Phase F. Phase F uses them as inputs for detailed planning. Also: the Architecture Roadmap is first produced in complete form in Phase E (as v0.1) and finalized in Phase F.

Phase F: Migration Planning

  • Goal: Finalize the Architecture Roadmap and produce the detailed Implementation and Migration Plan
  • Key Deliverables:
    • Implementation and Migration Plan (finalized) — detailed schedule with resource allocation, costs, sequencing
    • Finalized Architecture Roadmap — the definitive version of the roadmap
    • Architecture Contracts — formal agreements between the architecture team and implementation projects; establish compliance requirements
  • Inputs include: Transition Architectures (from Phase E), Work Packages (from Phase E)
  • Key Activity: Prioritize and sequence work packages; assign resources; finalize the migration plan and roadmap

Phase G: Implementation Governance

  • Goal: Ensure implementation projects comply with the agreed architecture
  • Key Deliverables:
    • Compliance Assessments — formal evaluations of how well each implementation project conforms to the target architecture
    • Architecture Change Requests — formal proposals for changes to the architecture raised during implementation
    • Implementation Reports — status and quality reports on ongoing implementation
    • Architecture Contracts (monitored and enforced here; originated in Phase F)
  • Key Activity: Monitor projects against architecture; manage non-conformances; control architecture changes during implementation

Exam tip: Phase G is the only phase where the architect is NOT designing architecture — they are governing implementation. The key tool is the Compliance Assessment.

Phase H: Architecture Change Management

  • Goal: Continuously monitor the deployed architecture and manage changes to keep it aligned with evolving business and technology
  • Key Deliverables:
    • Architecture Updates — updates to the Architecture Baseline when changes are approved
    • Change Decision Records — documented decisions on requested changes (approved/rejected/deferred)
    • New Request for Architecture Work — triggered when changes are significant enough to need a new ADM cycle
  • Key Activity: Monitor business and technology change triggers; evaluate change requests; decide whether minor updates suffice or a new ADM cycle is needed

Exam tip: Phase H loops back in one of three ways:

  • Stay in Phase H — minor changes handled without a new ADM cycle
  • Loop back to Phase A — significant new initiative requires a full new cycle
  • Loop back to Phase E or F — medium-scope changes that need re-planning but not full redesign

Key ADM Characteristics

  1. Iterative: You can run multiple ADM cycles in parallel
  2. Circular: Phase H loops back; may feed into new Phase A for the next initiative
  3. Customizable: You can skip phases, add phases, or reorder based on your needs
  4. Governance-driven: Each phase has decision points; progress is approved by architecture board

Requirements Management — The Center of the ADM Wheel

This is one of the most frequently missed concepts by students: Requirements Management is not a phase, it is a continuous process that runs through ALL ADM phases simultaneously.

In TOGAF diagrams, the ADM is shown as a wheel with 9 phases around the outside. Requirements Management sits at the center of the wheel, feeding into and receiving from every phase.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     ADM Wheel (simplified)                   │
│                                                              │
│    Prelim     A (Vision)     B (Business)     C (IS Arch)   │
│                   ┌─────────────────────┐                   │
│    H (Change) │   │  Requirements       │ │  D (Technology)  │
│               │   │  Management         │ │                  │
│    G (Gov)    │   │  (center — always   │ │  E (Opps)        │
│               └───│  running)           │─┘                  │
│    F (Migr)       └─────────────────────┘                   │
│                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

What Requirements Management does:

  • Captures requirements as they emerge in any phase
  • Ensures requirements are tracked throughout the full ADM cycle
  • Manages changes to requirements as the architecture evolves
  • Connects stakeholder needs to architecture decisions at every stage

Why this matters for the exam:

  • Exam question: "Which process runs continuously through all ADM phases?" → Requirements Management
  • Exam question: "Where does Requirements Management sit in the ADM?" → At the center of the ADM cycle
  • It is NOT a phase you complete and move past — it is always active

Key Takeaway for Day 3

The ADM has 9 phases (Preliminary + A–H) PLUS Requirements Management at the center running continuously. Master the sequence and the central role of Requirements Management.

Day 4: ADM Inputs & Outputs — What Flows Between Phases

Each ADM phase consumes inputs from the previous phase and produces outputs for the next phase.

The ADM Flow: Inputs → Phase Activity → Outputs

Current State Artifacts
+ Business/IT Strategies
+ Constraints
+ Change Requests
       │
       ▼
┌──────────────────────────┐
│   ADM Phase (A–H)        │
│  - Perform Analysis      │
│  - Make Decisions        │
│  - Create Artifacts      │
└──────────────────────────┘
       │
       ▼
Target State Artifacts
+ Architecture Models
+ Decisions Documented
+ Ready for Next Phase

Phase-by-Phase Input/Output Examples

Phase A: Architecture Vision

Inputs:

  • Request for Architecture Work — the formal trigger document that initiates Phase A; comes from business or IT leadership sponsoring the architecture effort (this is its exact TOGAF name — not just "a request")
  • Business Strategy, Business Goals, IT Strategy
  • Organizational constraints (resources, time, budget)
  • Existing architecture documentation (if any)
  • Stakeholder list and concerns

Activities:

  • Define problem scope
  • Identify and engage stakeholders
  • Create architecture vision statement
  • Define success criteria and constraints

Outputs:

  • Architecture Vision Statement — describes the target state at a high level
  • Statement of Architecture Work — the formal charter; defines scope, schedule, resources, and is signed off by the sponsoring executive (this is its exact TOGAF name — not just "charter")
  • Business Case for architecture program
  • Stakeholder Map & Concerns Analysis
  • Approved Architecture Vision

Flows to: Phase B

Exam tip: "Request for Architecture Work" triggers Phase A. "Statement of Architecture Work" is the formal output/charter from Phase A. These exact names appear in exam questions.

Phase B: Business Architecture

Inputs:

  • Architecture Vision (from Phase A)
  • Existing business process documentation
  • Organizational structure
  • Business process standards

Activities:

  • Model current business (AS-IS)
  • Design target business (TO-BE)
  • Document business capabilities
  • Define business metrics

Outputs:

  • Business Process Models (AS-IS & TO-BE)
  • Organizational Structure Diagrams
  • Business Capability Map
  • Business Glossary (partial)

Flows to: Phase C

Phase C: Information Systems Architecture

Inputs:

  • Business Architecture (from Phase B)
  • Existing data models and application inventory
  • Data governance policies
  • Integration standards

Activities:

  • Design data architecture (logical — technology-independent; physical data models are project-level, not EA-level)
  • Design application architecture
  • Map data to applications
  • Design system interfaces

Outputs:

  • Data Models (logical — NOT physical)
  • Application Portfolio Map
  • Application Interface Catalog
  • Data Flow Diagrams

Flows to: Phase D

Phase D: Technology Architecture

Inputs:

  • Information Systems Architecture (from Phase C)
  • Existing technology standards
  • Infrastructure capacity data
  • Technology vendor roadmaps

Activities:

  • Define technology standards
  • Design infrastructure stack
  • Define deployment patterns
  • Create technology roadmap

Outputs:

  • Technology Reference Architecture
  • Technology Standards & Roadmap
  • Infrastructure Diagrams
  • Platform Components List

Flows to: Phase E

Phase E: Opportunities & Solutions

Inputs:

  • Technology Architecture (from Phase D)
  • Gap Analysis results from Phases B, C, and D (consolidated here for the first time)
  • Budget constraints
  • Resource availability
  • Business priorities

Activities:

  • Consolidate gap analysis results across all 4 domains
  • Group related gaps into Work Packages
  • Define Transition Architectures (the intermediate stable states)
  • Assess business value vs. implementation risk for each Work Package
  • Produce the first complete Architecture Roadmap

Outputs:

  • Work Package List — each Work Package has scope, dependencies, benefit, and risk
  • Transition Architecture(s) — intermediate stable states between AS-IS and TO-BE (Phase E, not Phase F)
  • Architecture Roadmap v0.1 — first complete, integrated roadmap across all domains
  • Implementation and Migration Plan v0.1 — initial plan
  • Risk & Dependency Analysis

Flows to: Phase F

Exam tip: Transition Architectures and Architecture Roadmap v0.1 are produced in Phase E. Phase F finalizes and details them. A question asking "where are Transition Architectures first defined?" → Phase E.

Phase F: Migration Planning

Inputs:

  • Work Packages and Architecture Roadmap v0.1 (from Phase E)
  • Transition Architectures (from Phase E — defined there, used here for sequencing)
  • Current state of infrastructure
  • Change capacity of organization
  • Regulatory requirements

Activities:

  • Prioritize and sequence work packages against business value and risk
  • Create the detailed Implementation and Migration Plan
  • Finalize the Architecture Roadmap
  • Establish Architecture Contracts for implementation projects

Outputs:

  • Implementation and Migration Plan (finalized) — detailed schedule, resource allocation, costs
  • Finalized Architecture Roadmap — definitive, approved roadmap
  • Architecture Contracts — formal compliance agreements between architecture team and implementation projects
  • Implementation Schedule, Resource Plan

Flows to: Phase G

Exam tip: Transition Architectures are defined in Phase E, NOT Phase F. Phase F uses them as inputs. The key Phase F outputs are the finalized Implementation and Migration Plan and the finalized Architecture Roadmap — the word "finalized" distinguishes Phase F's outputs from Phase E's v0.1 versions.

Phase G: Implementation Governance

Inputs:

  • Migration Plan (from Phase F)
  • Architecture baseline
  • Governance policies
  • Project management standards

Activities:

  • Monitor implementation against architecture
  • Manage compliance issues
  • Control changes
  • Track risks and issues

Outputs:

  • Compliance & Impact Assessments
  • Issue & Risk Logs
  • Architecture Change Requests
  • Implementation Reports

Flows to: Phase H (or loops back for adjustments)

Phase H: Architecture Change Management

Inputs:

  • Implemented architecture (from Phase G)
  • Change requests from operations
  • Business strategy updates
  • Technology updates

Activities:

  • Monitor architecture against strategy
  • Evaluate change requests
  • Update architecture as needed
  • Document lessons learned

Outputs:

  • Updated Architecture Baseline
  • Change Decision Records
  • Lessons Learned Document
  • Input to next ADM cycle (Phase A or update)

Loops back to: Phase H (continuous management) or Phase A (new initiative)

Key Concept: Continuous Flow

In real organizations, you often have multiple ADM cycles running in parallel:

Timeline:
Q1 2026  │ Preliminary ──► Phase A ──► Phase B ──► Phase C
         │                                          
Q2 2026  │                Phase A ──► Phase B ──► Phase C ──► Phase D
         │ (new initiative)           
         │                                         
Q3 2026  │ Phase C ──► Phase D ──► Phase E ──► Phase F ──► Phase G
         │ (continuing from Q1)

Different projects advance at different speeds. The overall enterprise architecture evolves continuously.

Key Takeaway for Day 4

Each ADM phase has clear inputs and outputs. The outputs of one phase become the inputs to the next. This creates a logical flow of architecture development.

Day 5: The 4 Architecture Domains

TOGAF organizes architecture into 4 domains. These domains are interdependent — changes in one affect the others.

The 4 Architecture Domains

1. Business Architecture

  • What: The organization, its structure, processes, capabilities, goals
  • Who designs it: Business architects, business process analysts, organizational strategists
  • Key Artifacts:
    • Organizational hierarchy diagrams
    • Business process models (BPMN, flowcharts)
    • Business capability maps
    • Business goals & KPIs
    • Value streams
  • Concerns: How is the business organized? What does it do? How does it execute strategy?
  • Your angle: Leadership & organizational structure; how teams work
  • Phase created: Phase B (Business Architecture)

Example:
In a retail company: store structure, supply chain organization, sales process, customer service process, business goals (revenue, customer satisfaction)

2. Data Architecture

  • What: Data entities, their relationships, how data flows, data governance
  • Who designs it: Data architects, database administrators, data governance specialists
  • Key Artifacts:
    • Entity-relationship diagrams (ERDs)
    • Data flow diagrams
    • Data catalogs
    • Data lineage diagrams
    • Master data model
  • Concerns: What data does the business have? How is it structured? How does it flow? What are the dependencies?
  • Your angle: You have strong data architecture experience; this domain is your strength
  • Phase created: Phase C (Information Systems Architecture — Data part)

Example:
In the same retail company: customer data, product data, transaction data, inventory data; how they relate; how data flows from transaction systems to analytics

3. Application Architecture

  • What: The applications, their interfaces, integrations, portfolios
  • Who designs it: Application architects, solution architects, systems engineers
  • Key Artifacts:
    • Application portfolio map
    • Application interaction diagrams
    • Interface catalogs
    • Integration architecture
    • Application technology stack
  • Concerns: What applications support the business? How do they talk to each other? Which are redundant? What's the roadmap for retiring/replacing?
  • Your angle: You've designed microservices and APIs; this is familiar territory
  • Phase created: Phase C (Information Systems Architecture — Application part)

Example:
In the retail company: Point-of-Sale (POS) system, Inventory Management system, E-commerce platform, Business Intelligence system, CRM; how they integrate; which data flows between them

4. Technology Architecture

  • What: Infrastructure, platforms, standards, technology stack
  • Who designs it: Infrastructure architects, platform engineers, technology strategists
  • Key Artifacts:
    • Infrastructure diagrams
    • Technology standards matrix
    • Technology roadmap
    • Deployment architecture
    • Platform component catalog
  • Concerns: What hardware, software, platforms, and cloud services support the applications? What are the standards? What's the roadmap?
  • Your angle: You know cloud, microservices, databases, messaging — very relevant
  • Phase created: Phase D (Technology Architecture)

Example:
In the retail company: data center infrastructure, Azure cloud services, application servers, databases, messaging queues, security infrastructure; standardized on Azure, PostgreSQL, Kafka; roadmap to migrate from on-prem to cloud

How the 4 Domains Relate

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│          Business Architecture                      │
│  (Organization, Processes, Capabilities, Goals)     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                      │                              │
│                      ▼                              │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│   Data Architecture          Application Architecture
│   (Data, Entities,    ◄──────────────►  (Apps,
│    Relationships)                       Interfaces,
│                                         Integrations)
│                      │                              │
│                      ▼                              │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│         Technology Architecture                     │
│  (Infrastructure, Platforms, Cloud, Standards)      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Key Relationship Rules:
- Business defines WHAT the organization does
- Data & Applications define HOW the organization executes
- Technology defines WHAT RUNS the applications & data
- Changes in Business flow down to Technology

Domain Sequencing in ADM

Phase Domain Focus
Phase B Business Architecture (current & target)
Phase C Data Architecture + Application Architecture
Phase D Technology Architecture
Phase E–H Integration of all 4 across roadmap & implementation

Key Point: Business drives everything. You start with business (Phase B), then design data/applications to support business (Phase C), then infrastructure to run those applications (Phase D).

Views, Viewpoints, and Stakeholders — The TOGAF Chain

This chain connects stakeholders to architecture outputs and is one of the most exam-tested structural concepts in TOGAF:

STAKEHOLDER
    │
    │ has one or more
    ▼
CONCERN (what the stakeholder cares about)
    │
    │ is addressed by selecting a
    ▼
VIEWPOINT (a defined perspective/lens for creating a view)
    │
    │ is applied to the architecture to produce a
    ▼
VIEW (a specific representation of the architecture from that viewpoint)
    │
    │ is expressed as one or more
    ▼
ARTIFACT (the tangible output: diagram, matrix, catalog, table)

Example of the chain in action:

Element Example
Stakeholder Chief Information Security Officer (CISO)
Concern "How is sensitive data protected from unauthorized access?"
Viewpoint Security Viewpoint (rules for creating security-focused views)
View Security Architecture View (the specific representation created)
Artifact Data Security Diagram (showing data zones, access controls, encryption)

Why this matters for the exam:

  • A Viewpoint is NOT a diagram — it is a specification of how to create a view; a template
  • A View is NOT a viewpoint — it is an instance created by applying a viewpoint to the architecture
  • One viewpoint can generate many views (e.g., the Security Viewpoint applied to each business unit)
  • Exam question: "What is the relationship between a View and a Viewpoint?" → A view is created by applying a viewpoint to the architecture

Cross-Domain Example: E-commerce Transformation

Let's say a traditional retail company wants to launch e-commerce (a real business need).

Business Architecture Impact:

  • New business unit: E-commerce Division
  • New process: Online order fulfillment
  • New capability: Digital marketing
  • New KPI: Online conversion rate

Data Architecture Impact:

  • New data: customer clickstream (how users browse)
  • New relationship: product ↔ inventory at multiple fulfillment centers
  • New master data: unified customer identity (in-store + online)

Application Architecture Impact:

  • New application: E-commerce platform (storefront)
  • New interface: API between storefront and inventory system
  • Integration point: payment gateway integration
  • Decommission: old batch order processing

Technology Architecture Impact:

  • Cloud-based deployment (scalability for variable traffic)
  • CDN for static content delivery (performance)
  • Load balancers for high availability
  • Analytics database for clickstream analysis

All 4 domains changed because of 1 business change. This is why enterprise architecture matters.

Key Takeaway for Day 5

The 4 architecture domains are Business → Data/Application → Technology. Business drives the others. Changes cascade. You must understand all 4 and how they interact.

Day 6: Key Terminology — 42 Essential TOGAF Terms

Today, memorize the 42 essential TOGAF terms below (organized into 5 tiers). These are the vocabulary of the exam and the profession.

Tier 1: Absolute Core (Must Know Cold)

Term Definition Context
Architecture A formal description of a system, organized in a way that supports reasoning about the system's properties. Includes structure, relationships, principles, and governance. Foundation concept
Enterprise Architecture Architecture covering all aspects of an enterprise (business, data, applications, technology) to align with business strategy. Exam focus
Architecture Principles Fundamental governance rules that guide all architecture decisions. Established in the Preliminary Phase and applied throughout ADM. Examples: "Data is an Asset", "Technology Independence", "Single Source of Truth". Principles have: Name, Statement, Rationale, Implications. Heavily tested — Preliminary Phase output
Stakeholder Any person or group with an interest in or concern about the architecture. Examples: executives, users, IT staff, regulators. Critical for understanding viewpoints
Concern A specific interest a stakeholder has in the architecture. Example: a CFO's concern is cost; a security officer's concern is data protection. Concerns drive which viewpoints and views are created. Links stakeholder → viewpoint → view
Viewpoint A perspective or lens for viewing the architecture, tailored to specific stakeholder concerns. Examples: executive viewpoint, technical viewpoint, data owner viewpoint. Artifact creation
View A specific representation of the architecture created from a particular viewpoint, addressing stakeholder concerns. Example: a diagram showing data flow for the data owner. Deliverable
Artifact A tangible work product of the architecture. Examples: diagram, matrix, catalog, document, model. Key deliverable
Architecture Development Method (ADM) The repeatable, step-by-step process TOGAF provides for developing enterprise architecture. 9 phases + Requirements Management at center. Core of TOGAF
Requirements Management The continuous process at the center of the ADM wheel; captures, manages, and tracks requirements across all phases simultaneously. Not a phase — always active. Central to ADM
Architecture Board Governance body that makes decisions about architecture, approves changes, manages escalations. Part of the Architecture Capability Framework (Part VII). Governance
Chief Architect Person who leads the enterprise architecture function; reports to CIO or Chief Digital Officer. Leadership role

Tier 2: Domain-Specific & Key Formal Terms (Important)

Term Definition Context
Business Architecture Architecture of the business structure, processes, capabilities, and goals. Answers: How is the organization organized? What does it do? Domain 1 — Phase B
Data Architecture Architecture of data entities, relationships, flows, and governance. Answers: What data exists? How is it structured? How does it flow? Domain 2 — Phase C (first)
Application Architecture Architecture of applications, their functions, interfaces, and integrations. Answers: What applications run the business? How do they talk to each other? Domain 3 — Phase C (second)
Technology Architecture Architecture of infrastructure, platforms, standards, and technology stack. Answers: What runs the applications? What are the standards? Domain 4 — Phase D
Current Architecture (AS-IS) The architecture as it exists today (before change). Documented in Phase B, C, D as the baseline. Baseline
Target Architecture (TO-BE) The desired future state architecture (after transformation). Designed in Phase B, C, D. Goal
Transition Architecture Intermediate, stable, deployable architecture states between AS-IS and TO-BE. First defined in Phase E; used in Phase F for detailed planning. Allows phased delivery — each transition state is coherent enough to run the business while more work continues. Defined in Phase E, used in Phase F
Enterprise Continuum A classification system for architectures ranging from generic/reusable (Foundation) to organization-specific. Spectrum: Foundation → Common Systems → Industry → Organization-Specific. Explains how TOGAF's reference models are used as starting points. Part V — tested concept
Request for Architecture Work The formal document that triggers Phase A. Issued by business/IT leadership to commission the architecture work. It defines the problem, scope, and sponsor. Phase A input — exact name matters
Statement of Architecture Work The formal output of Phase A. Functions as the project charter. Defines the scope, schedule, resources, and constraints. Must be approved by the sponsoring executive before work proceeds. Phase A output — exact name matters

Tier 3: Artifact & Method (Important)

Term Definition Context
Building Block A reusable component of the architecture. TOGAF distinguishes two types — see ABB and SBB below. Architecture reuse
Architecture Building Block (ABB) A conceptual building block that defines WHAT is needed in the target architecture, without specifying the implementation. Example: "a payment processing service" (abstract). Target architecture design
Solution Building Block (SBB) A concrete implementation of an ABB — a specific product, system, or component that fulfills the ABB. Example: "Stripe API v3" implements the "payment processing service" ABB. Implementation planning
Architecture Pattern A recurring solution to a common architecture problem. Example: master-data-management pattern, event-driven microservices pattern. Design guidance
Architecture Contract A formal agreement between the architecture team and the implementation team (project/supplier). Defines: what must be delivered, quality standards, compliance requirements. Created in Phase F; monitored and enforced in Phase G. Phase F (created) → Phase G (enforced)
Architecture Requirements Specification Companion document to the Architecture Definition Document. Defines the quantitative requirements (measurable) that the architecture must meet — performance, security, availability. Complements ADD
Metamodel A model of models; defines the structure and relationships of architecture artifacts. From the Content Framework (Part IV). Content framework
Repository Central storage for all architecture artifacts, models, and metadata. Part of the Enterprise Continuum (Part V). Architecture governance
Architecture Governance Decision-making framework and enforcement mechanisms for architecture decisions. Defines who decides, how decisions are made, and how compliance is enforced. Part VII
RACI Matrix Responsibility Assignment Chart. Maps activities/decisions to people/roles: Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed. Governance tool
Gap Analysis Process of comparing current state (AS-IS) to target state (TO-BE) to identify what needs to change. Results categorized as: Added (new in target), Eliminated (removed from baseline), Changed (modified — sometimes called "Improve/Enhance"), or Retained (unchanged). Performed once per domain in Phases B, C, and D; consolidated in Phase E. Phases B, C, D → consolidated in E
Work Package A bundle of related work items that can be scheduled, resourced, and tracked. Output of Phase E; input to Phase F migration planning. Implementation

Tier 4: Process & Governance (Good to Know)

Term Definition Context
Architecture Definition Document (ADD) Comprehensive documentation of the architecture from all viewpoints. Main deliverable
Architecture Governance Handbook Document defining how architecture decisions are made, who decides, escalation paths. Governance guidance
Compliance Assessment Evaluation of how well current systems/projects conform to the target architecture. Phase G
Change Request Proposal for a modification to the architecture or a decision. Governance process
Architecture Review Assessment of architecture against standards, principles, and strategy. Quality control

Tier 5: Reference Models (Foundational Awareness)

Term Definition Context
Foundation Architecture (FA) The most generic level of the Architecture Continuum — fundamental technology services and building blocks applicable to any organization. Embodied by the Technical Reference Model (TRM). Reference framework (Part VI)
Technical Reference Model (TRM) A taxonomy of generic technology service categories (the Application Platform + Communications Infrastructure). Used in Phase D. Reference framework (Part VI)
III-RM (Integrated Information Infrastructure Reference Model) A reference model at the application level that supports "Boundaryless Information Flow" — how information moves across the enterprise. (Note: the TRM covers technology/platform services; the III-RM focuses on the application software needed for integrated information flow.) Reference framework (Part VI)

Week 1 Practice Quiz

20 Questions on Week 1 Topics
Time limit: 30 minutes
Passing score: 16/20 (80%)

Questions 1–5: TOGAF Overview & Purpose

Q1. What is the primary purpose of TOGAF?

A) To provide specific software implementations for enterprise systems
B) To provide a framework and methodology for developing enterprise architectures
C) To define the best technology stack for organizations
D) To replace IT governance frameworks like COBIT

Answer: B — TOGAF is a framework (methodology) for architecture development, not software, not technology selection, not a replacement for other governance.

Q2. Which of the following is NOT a main part of TOGAF?

A) Architecture Development Method (ADM)
B) Architecture Content Framework
C) Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC)
D) Reference Models

Answer: C — TOGAF 9.2 has 7 parts: Introduction (I), ADM (II), ADM Guidelines & Techniques (III), Architecture Content Framework (IV), Enterprise Continuum & Tools (V), Reference Models (VI), and Architecture Capability Framework (VII). SDLC is not part of TOGAF and never appears in the framework.

Q3. What is the main output of the Preliminary Phase of TOGAF ADM?

A) Architecture Vision Statement
B) Business Process Models
C) Architecture Governance Framework and tailored TOGAF methodology
D) Technology Roadmap

Answer: C — The Preliminary Phase sets up governance and customizes TOGAF before the architecture project begins.

Q4. Which of the following best describes the relationship between TOGAF and an organization's business strategy?

A) TOGAF replaces business strategy
B) TOGAF translates business strategy into architecture
C) TOGAF is independent of business strategy
D) TOGAF is only for IT, not business

Answer: B — A core principle of TOGAF is alignment: business strategy drives architecture.

Q5. Why would an organization use TOGAF instead of designing architecture ad-hoc?

A) TOGAF guarantees the cheapest solution
B) TOGAF provides a standardized, repeatable methodology that aligns architecture with business strategy and enables governance
C) TOGAF requires no stakeholder input
D) TOGAF automatically designs the entire system

Answer: B — TOGAF's value is standardization, repeatability, alignment, and governance.

Questions 6–10: ADM Phases & Sequencing

Q6. In which ADM phase is the Business Process Model created?

A) Preliminary
B) Phase A: Architecture Vision
C) Phase B: Business Architecture
D) Phase C: Information Systems Architecture

Answer: C — "Phase B: Business Architecture" — Business Process Models are a core output of Phase B. Note: option C is labeled "Phase B" — don't confuse the option letter with the phase name.

Q7. Which phase follows Phase E (Opportunities & Solutions) in the ADM sequence?

A) Phase D: Technology Architecture
B) Phase F: Migration Planning
C) Phase G: Implementation Governance
D) Phase H: Architecture Change Management

Answer: B — The correct sequence is A → B → C → D → E → F → G → H.

Q8. What is the PRIMARY purpose of Phase H (Architecture Change Management)?

A) To execute the implementation of the architecture
B) To continuously monitor and manage the architecture after go-live
C) To plan the migration timeline
D) To design the technology infrastructure

Answer: B — Phase H ensures the architecture remains relevant; it's continuous monitoring, not one-time implementation.

Q9. Which of the following is an output of Phase E (Opportunities & Solutions)?

A) Data Models
B) Technology Roadmap
C) Work Package List and Implementation Roadmap
D) Compliance Assessment

Answer: C — Phase E identifies what work needs to be done and in what order.

Q10. An organization can skip phases in the ADM if they don't apply. This is an example of which TOGAF principle?

A) Governance
B) Customization
C) Mandatory completion
D) Phase sequencing

Answer: B — TOGAF allows customization to fit your organization's needs.

Questions 11–15: Architecture Domains

Q11. Which architecture domain focuses on how the organization is structured and what business processes it performs?

A) Data Architecture
B) Application Architecture
C) Business Architecture
D) Technology Architecture

Answer: C — Business Architecture covers organization, processes, capabilities, and goals.

Q12. A company wants to implement a new master data management (MDM) system. Which architecture domain is PRIMARY in designing this?

A) Business Architecture
B) Data Architecture
C) Application Architecture
D) Technology Architecture

Answer: B — MDM is fundamentally a data architecture concern (managing master records across systems).

Q13. Which of the following is a typical artifact of Technology Architecture?

A) Business Process Model
B) Entity-Relationship Diagram (ERD)
C) Technology Standards & Infrastructure Diagram
D) Application Portfolio Map

Answer: C — Technology Architecture produces infrastructure diagrams and standards.

Q14. In which ADM phase is the Technology Architecture domain typically designed?

A) Phase B
B) Phase C
C) Phase D
D) Phase E

Answer: C — "Phase D: Technology Architecture" — Phase D is specifically for Technology Architecture. Note: option C is labeled "Phase D" — don't confuse the option letter with the phase name.

Q15. Which statement BEST describes the relationship between Application Architecture and Technology Architecture?

A) They are independent; applications don't depend on technology
B) Applications run ON technology; application design depends on technology constraints
C) Technology architecture is designed first; application architecture follows
D) They are the same thing

Answer: B — Applications are deployed on technology platforms; there's a dependency relationship.

Questions 16–20: Terminology & Concepts

Q16. What is a "Viewpoint" in TOGAF?

A) A diagram type
B) A perspective or lens tailored to specific stakeholder concerns
C) An implementation tool
D) A governance role

Answer: B — Viewpoint is TOGAF's way of creating perspectives for different stakeholders.

Q17. Which of the following is the purpose of an Architecture Repository?

A) To store software code
B) To centrally store and manage architecture artifacts, models, and metadata
C) To execute the architecture
D) To approve architecture changes

Answer: B — Repository is the central storage for all architecture work.

Q18. What does RACI stand for?

A) Requirements, Analysis, Change, Implementation
B) Risk, Assessment, Compliance, Infrastructure
C) Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed
D) Review, Approve, Certify, Integrate

Answer: C — RACI is a responsibility assignment matrix.

Q19. Which role has ultimate accountability for architecture decisions?

A) Chief Architect
B) Business Process Owner
C) Architecture Board
D) CIO

Answer: C — The Architecture Board is the governance body that makes decisions.

Q20. A "Building Block" in TOGAF is best described as:

A) A physical server or computer
B) A reusable component of the architecture (could be data, application, or technology)
C) A project deliverable
D) A risk management tool

Answer: B — Building blocks are reusable architecture components.

Bonus Questions (Extra Practice)

Q21. Which of the following BEST describes Requirements Management in the TOGAF ADM?

A) A phase that runs between Phase A and Phase B
B) A process that runs continuously through all ADM phases simultaneously
C) A technique used only during Phase E
D) A governance role held by the Architecture Board

Answer: B — Requirements Management sits at the center of the ADM wheel and runs continuously through all phases. It is not a phase; it is always active.

Q22. A company wants to implement an e-commerce platform and is using TOGAF. They find a relevant industry reference architecture from a retail consortium. According to TOGAF, what concept describes this spectrum from generic to organization-specific architectures?

A) Architecture Landscape
B) Architecture Repository
C) Enterprise Continuum
D) Architecture Capability Framework

Answer: C — The Enterprise Continuum classifies architectures from generic (Foundation Architecture) to organization-specific. A retail consortium architecture sits in the "Industry Architecture" band of the continuum.

Q23. What is the difference between a "Request for Architecture Work" and a "Statement of Architecture Work"?

A) They are different names for the same document
B) The Request triggers Phase A; the Statement is the formal charter output of Phase A
C) The Request is produced in Phase B; the Statement is produced in Phase A
D) The Statement triggers Phase A; the Request is the output

Answer: B — Request for Architecture Work is the formal input trigger that starts Phase A. Statement of Architecture Work is the formal output/charter that Phase A produces, approved by the sponsoring executive.

Q24. Which of the following BEST distinguishes an Architecture Building Block (ABB) from a Solution Building Block (SBB)?

A) ABBs are used in Technology Architecture; SBBs are used in Business Architecture
B) ABBs define what is needed conceptually; SBBs define the specific implementation
C) SBBs are created first; ABBs are created during implementation
D) There is no meaningful difference; the terms are interchangeable

Answer: B — ABBs are conceptual ("a payment service is needed"); SBBs are concrete implementations ("Stripe API v3 fulfills this"). ABBs are defined in the target architecture design; SBBs are selected/built during implementation planning.

Q25. Architecture Principles established in the Preliminary Phase have four components. Which of the following is NOT one of the four components?

A) Name
B) Statement
C) Priority
D) Implications

Answer: C — Priority is not one of the four components. The four are: Name (label), Statement (the rule), Rationale (why it matters, the business benefit), and Implications (what following the principle requires from business and IT). Principles do not have a priority ranking in TOGAF.

Q26. An organization is implementing TOGAF for the first time. Before starting any architecture project, the architecture team defines governance processes, customizes the TOGAF framework to fit the organization's methods, and establishes architecture principles. Which ADM phase are they in?

A) Phase A: Architecture Vision
B) Phase B: Business Architecture
C) Preliminary Phase
D) Phase H: Architecture Change Management

Answer: C — Preliminary Phase — all of these activities (tailoring the framework, establishing governance, creating architecture principles) are Preliminary Phase activities. They happen BEFORE any specific architecture project begins. Phase A starts a specific project; the Preliminary Phase sets up the capability to do architecture.

Q27. In TOGAF, a Viewpoint and a View are related but distinct concepts. Which of the following BEST describes this relationship?

A) A View and a Viewpoint are the same thing — different names for the same artifact
B) A Viewpoint is a template/specification; applying it to the architecture creates a View
C) A View is created first; the Viewpoint documents how the View was made
D) Viewpoints are for technical stakeholders; Views are for business stakeholders

Answer: B — A Viewpoint defines the rules and conventions for creating a particular kind of view (it is a template). A View is the actual representation of the architecture created by applying a viewpoint. The chain is: Stakeholder → Concern → Viewpoint → View → Artifact. One viewpoint can be used to create many views.

ADM Phases

  • Explain why Business (Phase B) must come before Data/Application (Phase C) which must come before Technology (Phase D)

  • Know that Transition Architectures are first defined in Phase E (not Phase F)

  • Know that Gap Analysis is performed in Phases B, C, D (not Phase E); Phase E consolidates results
  • Know that Phase G output is Compliance Assessments (not "oversight/QA")
  • Know that Phase H loops back to Phase A (new initiative), or E/F (medium change), or stays in H (minor)

The 9 ADM Phases (In Sequence)

Preliminary → A → B → C → D → E → F → G → H → (loops)
Phase Name What's Designed Key Output
Preliminary Framework & Governance How TOGAF will be customized Governance framework
A Architecture Vision Problem definition & stakeholder alignment Vision statement, Business case
B Business Architecture Business structure, processes, goals Org chart, Process models
C Information Systems Architecture Data & applications Data models, App portfolio
D Technology Architecture Infrastructure & platforms Tech standards, Infrastructure
E Opportunities & Solutions What work needs to be done Work packages, Roadmap
F Migration Planning Sequencing & prioritization Migration plan, Timeline
G Implementation Governance Oversight during execution Compliance assessments
H Architecture Change Management Monitoring post-go-live Change decisions, Updates

TOGAF Quick Facts

  • What: Framework for developing enterprise architecture
  • Goal: Align business strategy with IT through structured methodology
  • Exam: 40 questions, 60 minutes, 60% pass (24/40)
  • Your preparation: 8 weeks intensive, 3 hrs/day
  • ADM is: ~60% of exam; the core
  • Domains are: ~10% of exam; you know 90% already
  • Critical to master: ADM phases, domain relationships, key artifacts

30 Essential Terms (Quick Definitions)

  1. Architecture — Formal description of a system with structure, relationships, and governance
  2. Enterprise Architecture — Architecture covering all business, data, application, and technology aspects
  3. Stakeholder — Anyone with an interest in or concern about the architecture
  4. Viewpoint — A perspective tailored to specific stakeholder concerns
  5. View — A specific representation of architecture from a particular viewpoint
  6. Artifact — Tangible output: diagram, matrix, catalog, document
  7. ADM — The 9-phase Architecture Development Method
  8. Architecture Board — Governance body that approves architecture decisions
  9. Chief Architect — Leader of enterprise architecture function
  10. Business Architecture — Architecture of org structure, processes, capabilities, goals
  11. Data Architecture — Architecture of data entities, flows, governance
  12. Application Architecture — Architecture of applications, interfaces, integrations
  13. Technology Architecture — Architecture of infrastructure, platforms, standards
  14. AS-IS — Current architecture (before change)
  15. TO-BE — Target architecture (desired future state)
  16. Transition Architecture — Intermediate states during migration
  17. Building Block — Reusable architecture component
  18. Architecture Pattern — Recurring solution to common architecture problem
  19. Metamodel — Model defining structure of architecture artifacts
  20. Repository — Central storage for all architecture work
  21. Architecture Governance — Decision-making and enforcement for architecture
  22. RACI Matrix — Maps activities to: Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed
  23. Gap Analysis — Comparing current vs. target to identify what must change
  24. Work Package — Bundle of related work items
  25. Architecture Definition Document (ADD) — Main architecture documentation
  26. Governance Handbook — Defines how architecture decisions are made
  27. Compliance Assessment — Evaluation of conformance to target architecture
  28. Change Request — Proposal to modify architecture or decision
  29. Architecture Review — Assessment of architecture against standards
  30. Foundation Architecture (FA) — TOGAF's reference model for enterprise
